theme_zh: 專案啟動會議：把方向講清楚、提出建議
summary_zh: 學會在專案啟動會議中用 Why don't we… / I'd suggest that… 有禮貌地提出建議，並把交付項目、窗口和進度回報方式講清楚。

vocab.definition: to start a meeting, project or event
vocab.example: We'll kick off the project with a two-hour workshop on Monday.
vocab.example_zh: 我們週一會用兩小時的工作坊啟動這個專案。

vocab.definition: a specific piece of work that must be finished and handed over as part of a project
vocab.example: The main deliverable for this phase is a working prototype.
vocab.example_zh: 這個階段主要的交付項目是一個可以運作的原型。

vocab.definition: approximate; not exact but close enough to plan with
vocab.example: Can you give me a ballpark figure for the budget?
vocab.example_zh: 你可以給我一個預算的大概數字嗎？

vocab.definition: the person you should go to with questions about a particular area
vocab.example: Anna will be our point of contact for anything related to design.
vocab.example_zh: 跟設計有關的事，Anna 會是我們的窗口。

vocab.definition: a point in a process where work slows down because too much depends on one person or step
vocab.example: Legal review has become a bottleneck, so contracts are taking weeks to sign.
vocab.example_zh: 法務審查變成了瓶頸，所以合約要好幾週才簽得下來。

vocab.zh: 簡短聯絡、確認一下近況
vocab.definition: to talk to someone briefly to share updates or check how things are going
vocab.example: Let's touch base on Friday to see where we are.
vocab.example_zh: 我們週五簡單對一下，看看進度到哪裡。

vocab.zh: 取得（大家的）認同與支持
vocab.definition: to get people to agree with and support a plan or decision
vocab.example: It's hard to get buy-in from other teams if they don't understand why the project matters.
vocab.example_zh: 如果其他團隊不懂這個專案為什麼重要，就很難取得他們的支持。

vocab.definition: to start something new and make progress immediately, without needing time to get ready
vocab.example: The new engineer had read all the docs, so she hit the ground running on day one.
vocab.example_zh: 新來的工程師把文件都讀完了，所以第一天就馬上進入狀況。

reading.title: How to Run a Kickoff Meeting That Actually Works
paragraphs: Most projects don't fail in the final week. They fail quietly in the first one, when nobody is quite sure who owns what. That's why a good kickoff meeting matters more than most teams think. It's the one moment when everyone is in the same room, the plan is still flexible, and people are still willing to speak up.

Start with the why, not the how. Before anyone opens a spreadsheet, the project lead should explain in two or three sentences what problem the project solves and what success looks like. Then move on to the deliverables: what exactly will the team hand over, and by when? Rough dates are fine at this stage. A ballpark timeline that everyone understands is more useful than a detailed one that nobody has read.

Next, name a point of contact for each area. When questions come up later, people should know exactly who to ask instead of sending messages to the whole group. This is also the time to look for bottlenecks. If one designer has to approve every screen, that person will slow the whole project down, so it's better to raise the issue now than in week six.

Finally, agree on how often you'll touch base. A short weekly check-in is usually enough to keep things on track, with a longer review at each milestone. Good project leads also tend to end the meeting with suggestions rather than orders: "Why don't we try weekly updates for the first month and see how it goes?" Phrasing it this way makes it much easier to get buy-in from people who don't report to you.

A team that leaves the kickoff with clear goals, owners and check-ins can hit the ground running. A team that leaves with vague promises usually spends the next month working out what it was supposed to be doing.

questions.q: According to the writer, when do most projects start to go wrong?
options: In the final week, when the deadline gets close
In the first week, when it isn't clear who is responsible for what
At each milestone review
When the budget is approved
questions.explain_zh: 第一段：「They fail quietly in the first one, when nobody is quite sure who owns what.」專案是在第一週、權責不清時就悄悄出問題。

questions.q: Why does the writer recommend naming a point of contact for each area?
options: So the project lead doesn't have to attend every meeting
So that one person can approve every screen
So people know who to ask instead of messaging the whole group
So the team can finish the project faster than planned
questions.explain_zh: 第三段：「people should know exactly who to ask instead of sending messages to the whole group.」

questions.q: Why might phrasing plans as suggestions help with people who "don't report to you"?
options: Because you can't just give them orders, so you need them to agree
Because suggestions are shorter than orders
Because those people usually don't attend kickoff meetings
Because managers are not allowed to give orders in meetings
questions.explain_zh: 推論題：不是你的部屬，你就沒有權力下命令；用「Why don't we…?」這種建議的方式，讓對方覺得被尊重、有參與感，比較容易取得支持（get buy-in）。

grammar.point: Making suggestions: Why don't we… / I'd suggest that…
grammar.point_zh: 提出建議：Why don't we… / I'd suggest that…
grammar.explain_zh: Why don't we + 原形動詞？是口語又友善的提議，不是真的在問「為什麼」；How about / What about + V-ing 也很常用。比較正式時用 I'd suggest that + 主詞 + 原形動詞（that 子句裡的動詞用原形，第三人稱也不加 s），或 I'd suggest + V-ing。對照組：✗ I suggest you to send it. → ✓ I'd suggest (that) you send it. ／ ✓ I'd suggest sending it.；✗ Why we don't…? → ✓ Why don't we…?
grammar.pattern: Why don't we + V? / I'd suggest (that) + S + V（原形） / I'd suggest + V-ing

examples.en: Why don't we set up a quick call with the client before we finalize the timeline?
examples.zh: 我們何不在確定時程前，先跟客戶開個簡短的電話會議？

examples.en: I'd suggest that each team name one point of contact.
examples.zh: 我建議每個團隊指定一位窗口。

examples.en: I'd suggest starting with a smaller pilot and expanding it later.
examples.zh: 我建議先從小規模試行開始，之後再擴大。

exercises.q: ___ we split the work into two phases? (提議：我們何不…？)
exercises.explain_zh: Why don't we + 原形動詞？是友善的提議，don't 放在 we 前面（不是 Why we don't）。

exercises.q: I'd suggest that she ___ the client before Friday.
options: calls
call
to call
calling
exercises.explain_zh: suggest that 子句的動詞用原形（美式與正式英文的標準用法），主詞是 she 也不加 s，所以是 call。英式英文也常說 calls 或 should call，但本課以美式為準，請用原形。

options: I suggest you to update the timeline.
I'd suggest updating the timeline.
I'd suggest to update the timeline.
I suggest you updating the timeline.
exercises.explain_zh: suggest 後面接 V-ing 或 that 子句，不接 to V，也不接「人 + to V」。正確是 I'd suggest updating…

exercises.q: How about ___ (move) the review to Thursday?
exercises.explain_zh: How about / What about 後面接 V-ing。

exercises.q: You're in a meeting with a senior manager from another department. Which suggestion sounds the most polite?
options: We have to change the plan.
Change the plan.
I'd suggest that we take another look at the plan.
Why you don't change the plan?
exercises.explain_zh: I'd suggest that we… 語氣委婉又正式；A、B 像命令；D 語序錯誤，應該是 Why don't you…?

exercises.q: I'd suggest that he ___ (touch) base with the design team before the next milestone.
exercises.explain_zh: suggest that 子句用原形動詞，主詞是 he 也不加 s。

review.point: Present perfect continuous for ongoing situations
review.point_zh: 現在完成進行式：描述「從過去一直持續到現在」的狀況（對照：過去的時間點 → 過去式）

exercises.q: We ___ (work) on this proposal since September, and it still isn't finished.
exercises.explain_zh: since September 到現在還在做（still isn't finished），用 have been + V-ing。

exercises.q: I ___ the report yesterday afternoon, so you should have it already.
options: have been finishing
finished
have finished
am finishing
exercises.explain_zh: 有明確的過去時間點 yesterday afternoon → 用過去式 finished。時間點用過去式、持續到現在才用完成（進行）式。

exercises.q: "Sorry I'm late! ___ long?" — "No, just a few minutes."
options: Have you been waiting
Do you wait
Are you waiting
Had you been waiting
exercises.explain_zh: 對方從過去等到現在（剛剛還在等），問「你等很久了嗎」用現在完成進行式 Have you been waiting long?

listening.title: The first project meeting

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Ethan
lines.text: Thanks for joining, everyone. Before we kick off, I'd like to make sure we all agree on the main deliverables.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Priya
lines.text: Sure. From the client's side, they mainly want the new dashboard and a short training video.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Ethan
lines.text: Right. Do we have a ballpark date for the dashboard?

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Priya
lines.text: They mentioned mid-January, but honestly, design could be a bottleneck. Our only designer is already on two other projects.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Ethan
lines.text: Good point. Why don't we ask Lena to join as a second designer for the first month?

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Priya
lines.text: That would really help. I'd also suggest that we have one point of contact on the client side, so we don't get five different opinions.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Ethan
lines.text: Agreed. Could you reach out to them and ask who that should be?

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Priya
lines.text: I'll do it this afternoon. How often do you want to touch base?

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Ethan
lines.text: Let's do a fifteen-minute check-in every Tuesday, and a longer review at each milestone.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Priya
lines.text: Sounds good. If we keep things that simple, we should be able to stay on track.

questions.q: What are the two main deliverables the client wants?
options: A dashboard and a training video
A website and a mobile app
A dashboard and a weekly report
A training video and a new design system
questions.explain_zh: Priya 說：「they mainly want the new dashboard and a short training video.」

questions.q: Why might design become a bottleneck?
options: The client keeps changing the design
The only designer is already working on two other projects
Lena doesn't want to join the team
The dashboard is due before mid-January
questions.explain_zh: Priya 說：「Our only designer is already on two other projects.」唯一的設計師同時做三個專案，所以可能卡住。

questions.q: Why does Priya want just one point of contact on the client side?
options: Because the client is too busy to attend meetings
Because she wants to cut down on the number of meetings
To avoid getting conflicting feedback from several people
Because Ethan asked her to find a new designer
questions.explain_zh: 推論題：她說「so we don't get five different opinions」——窗口太多會收到互相矛盾的意見，所以只要一個窗口。

dictation: Do we have a ballpark date for the dashboard?
Why don't we ask Lena to join as a second designer for the first month?
Let's do a fifteen-minute check-in every Tuesday, and a longer review at each milestone.

shadowing: Before we kick off, let's agree on the main deliverables.
Why don't we touch base again on Friday?
I'd suggest that we name one point of contact for each team.
If we keep it simple, we can hit the ground running.

prompts.question: Your team is starting a new project, but nobody is sure who is responsible for what. Make two or three suggestions.
prompts.question_zh: 團隊要開始一個新專案，但大家不清楚誰負責什麼。提出兩三個建議。
prompts.sample: Why don't we start by listing the main deliverables and putting a name next to each one? I'd also suggest that every team choose one point of contact, so people know exactly who to ask. And how about a short check-in every Monday, at least for the first month?

prompts.question: Think about a project you're working on now. What have you been doing on it lately, and what would you suggest changing?
prompts.question_zh: 想一個你目前在做的專案：你最近一直在做什麼？你會建議改變什麼？
prompts.sample: Lately, I've been spending a lot of time on reports for the client. One bottleneck is that every report has to be approved by my manager, and she's been really busy. I'd suggest letting senior team members approve the smaller reports, so we can move faster.

writing.task: Write a short message to your team after a project kickoff meeting. Sum up the main deliverables and make two suggestions for how the team should work together.
writing.task_zh: 專案啟動會議結束後，寫一則簡短訊息給團隊：整理主要的交付項目，並提出兩個團隊合作方式的建議。
writing.sample: Hi everyone, thanks for a great kickoff today. Just to sum up, our two main deliverables are the new customer dashboard, due in mid-January, and a short training video for the client's staff. I have two suggestions for how we work together. First, why don't we keep all project questions in one shared channel instead of sending private messages? That way, nobody misses an update. Second, I'd suggest that we touch base every Tuesday for fifteen minutes, just to check progress and raise any problems early. Let me know if you have other ideas. Thanks, Ethan
checklist_zh: 先用一兩句整理交付項目與大概時程
用 Why don't we + 原形動詞 提出一個建議
用 I'd suggest that + 主詞 + 原形動詞 提出另一個建議
語氣友善，結尾邀請大家提供意見

translation.zh: 我們何不先開個短會，把主要的交付項目講清楚？
translation.en: Why don't we have a quick meeting first to clarify the main deliverables?
alt: Why don't we start with a short meeting to make the main deliverables clear?
Why don't we have a short meeting first to go over the main deliverables?

translation.zh: 我建議每個部門指定一位窗口。
translation.en: I'd suggest that each department name a point of contact.
alt: I'd suggest that each department choose a point of contact.
I suggest that each department appoint a point of contact.

translation.zh: 這兩個禮拜我們一直在準備專案啟動會議。
translation.en: We've been preparing for the project kickoff meeting for the past two weeks.
alt: For the last two weeks, we've been getting ready for the project kickoff.
We've been preparing for the kickoff meeting for two weeks.

reading.title: The Kickoff That Almost Went Off the Rails
paragraphs: When Maya was asked to lead the kickoff for her company's new customer portal, she assumed the hard part would be the timeline. It turned out to be the people. Within ten minutes, the head of sales had taken over the meeting, rattling off feature requests as if the scope had already been agreed on. The engineers went quiet, the designer stared at her laptop, and Maya could feel the project slipping out of her hands before it had even started.

Her first instinct was to push back head-on. Instead, she bit her tongue and waited for a natural pause. "These are all great ideas," she said. "Why don't we park them for a minute and agree on what has to be ready for launch? Everything else can go on a wish list." Nobody could really argue with that, and the head of sales, to his credit, sat back and let the others weigh in.

Then came the touchy subject of resources. Maya knew the engineering team was already stretched thin, but she also knew that saying so bluntly would sound like complaining. So she framed it as a suggestion: "I'd suggest that we revisit the launch date once we've seen the first prototype. That way, we're not committing to something we can't deliver." It was a small shift in wording, but it turned a potential argument into a shared decision.

Looking back, Maya says the meeting taught her that a kickoff isn't really about the plan. It's about setting the tone. If people leave feeling heard, they're far more likely to raise problems early instead of sitting on them until the deadline. If they leave feeling steamrolled, they'll nod along in meetings and then quietly do things their own way.
Six months later, the portal launched just two weeks behind the original ballpark date — which, by the company's standards, counted as a minor miracle.

questions.q: What can we infer about the engineers and the designer when the head of sales took over?
options: They agreed with every feature he suggested
They didn't feel comfortable speaking up
They were busy fixing a bug during the meeting
They had already finished the prototype
questions.explain_zh: 推論題：「The engineers went quiet, the designer stared at her laptop」——沉默、盯著電腦，表示他們覺得插不上話、不敢發言。

questions.q: Why did Maya suggest putting some ideas on a "wish list"?
options: To let the head of sales decide which features to build first
To make the launch date earlier
To separate launch essentials from nice-to-haves without dismissing anyone
Because the client had already rejected those features
questions.explain_zh: 她說先「agree on what has to be ready for launch」，其他放進 wish list——區分上線必備和加分功能，又不直接否定對方的點子。

questions.q: What does the last sentence suggest about the company's past projects?
options: They were usually delivered much later than planned
They were usually finished early
They never had a ballpark date
They were always led by the head of sales
questions.explain_zh: 推論題：只晚兩週就被稱為「a minor miracle」，暗示這家公司以前的專案通常延誤得更嚴重。

listening.title: Sorting out the budget

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Grace
lines.text: Okay, before we move on — has anyone actually confirmed the budget with finance?

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Tom
lines.text: Uh, sort of. They gave us a rough number, but they want a proper breakdown by the end of the month.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Grace
lines.text: The end of the month? That's... tight, considering we haven't even agreed on the scope.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Tom
lines.text: I know, I know. Look, why don't we just send them the estimate we have and—

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Grace
lines.text: And then get stuck with it? No, I'd rather we didn't lock ourselves into a number we can't defend.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Tom
lines.text: Fair enough. So what would you suggest?

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Grace
lines.text: I'd suggest that we split it into two phases. We give them a firm figure for phase one and a range for phase two.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Tom
lines.text: Hmm, they might not love the range, though. Finance likes things in black and white.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Grace
lines.text: Sure, but if we explain that phase two depends on the user research, it's hard to argue with.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Tom
lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Should I bring in Mark? He's been dealing with finance all year.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Grace
lines.text: Yes, definitely. Can you set up a call with him before Thursday?

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Tom
lines.text: On it. I'll send an invite as soon as we're done here.

questions.q: Why doesn't Grace want to send finance the current estimate?
options: It's already out of date
They might be stuck with a number they can't justify later
Finance has asked for a range instead
Tom made several mistakes in it
questions.explain_zh: Grace 說：「And then get stuck with it? … I'd rather we didn't lock ourselves into a number we can't defend.」怕被一個說不出依據的數字綁住。

options: Waiting until the scope is agreed before sending anything
Asking finance for a bigger budget
A fixed figure for phase one and a range for phase two
Letting Mark write the whole budget
questions.explain_zh: 她說：「We give them a firm figure for phase one and a range for phase two.」

questions.q: Why does Tom most likely want to bring in Mark?
options: Mark has experience with finance and can help them make their case
Mark is in charge of the user research
Mark wrote the original estimate
Mark is Grace's manager
questions.explain_zh: 推論題：Tom 說「He's been dealing with finance all year.」——Mark 熟悉財務部門，能幫忙說服對方接受分階段的預算。

dictation: I'd rather we didn't lock ourselves into a number we can't defend.
Finance likes things in black and white.
He's been dealing with finance all year.

glossary.zh: 一口氣快速說出（一連串）
glossary.definition: to say a list of things quickly, without stopping to think
stopped yourself from saying something you wanted to say (past tense of "bite your tongue")
to give your opinion in a discussion
having too much work and not enough people or time to do it

glossary.zh: 強壓、不讓別人表達意見
glossary.definition: to force people to accept something without listening to them
clearly stated, with no room for doubt
